assessment: SOURCE 1–2 show the same elongated building from its ramped short end and adjoining long side: a recessed lower frame, projecting two-level glazed enclosure, zigzag exterior ramps and a concave timber roof with unequal edge heights. SOURCE 3 shows the glazed entrance and an open gallery beneath grating supported by transverse beams. SOURCE 4 shows the curved timber ceiling, guarded circular floor openings, spiral stair and lower concrete-framed workspace. SOURCE 5–8 establish the perimeter buffer, retained frame, added upper hall and differing floor/void relationships through sections, exploded diagrams and plans; these are not exterior cutaway views. CURRENT captures the broad arrangement, but reverses defining end relationships, substitutes solid gallery construction and leaves a visible floor opening unguarded. No confirmed dimensions are supplied. The blank lower-interior image and repeated uncut views cannot verify internal floor connections or concealed joints.

issues.problem: SOURCE 1’s end views show the roof’s right edge higher than its left and the upper ramp descending toward the right. CURRENT 15 shows the opposite roof-edge hierarchy and upper-ramp direction. Ramp/rail extensions also project beyond the enclosure without clearly resolved landing connections.
issues.action: Locally correct the roof edge heights and ramp handedness against the same source end landmarks. Trim extensions and connect each flight to its corresponding landing with continuous walking surfaces and guards; preserve the established concave roof concept.

issues.problem: SOURCE 3 shows a light, permeable grating deck overhead with distinct transverse support beams. CURRENT 19 presents a continuous solid soffit with no comparable exposed beam rhythm. CURRENT 16–18 also read as heavy dark railing grids and opaque horizontal bands, obscuring the source’s light glazed buffer and open gallery.
issues.action: Patch the gallery deck to show the source-backed grating and exposed support bays. Reduce excessive rail/frame bulk and apply the observed pale frame finish and transparent glazing, retaining actual floor-edge structure.

issues.problem: SOURCE 4 shows mesh guards surrounding the visible circular floor openings. CURRENT 20 has a large foreground opening with no perimeter guard, while the farther stair opening has a coarse bar enclosure. The foreground opening’s exact placement cannot be confirmed from this camera.
issues.action: Add a continuous mesh guard around the exposed foreground opening and refine the stair-opening guard to the source’s light assembly. Check opening locations against SOURCE 7 before changing their positions; verify that stair flights terminate at real floor openings.

keep: The upper hall’s visible timber ceiling material zone.
The repeated pale columns along the lower glazed frontage.

assessment: SOURCE 1–2 establish the same elongated building through its zigzag ramp end, projecting two-level glazed perimeter and curved roof. SOURCE 3 shows recessed lower glazing and exposed columns beneath projecting walkways; SOURCE 4 shows the timber roof underside, open interior and spiral stair. SOURCE 5–8 provide sections, plans and assembly diagrams showing the retained frame, added roof storey and outer buffer zone. CURRENT contains these broad exterior systems, but its roof-to-enclosure proportions differ visibly. The ramp-end view also shows unresolved landing connections. Repeated uncut obliques do not verify the source interior, floor voids or stair arrangement. No confirmed dimensions are supplied; screenshots cannot establish actual joint connectivity or hidden geometry.

issues.problem: In SOURCE 1–2, the roof’s lowest central edge remains appreciably above the horizontal outer enclosure top, leaving a visible band of upper-storey glazing. In CURRENT 15, that central edge nearly meets the enclosure top, compressing this defining glazed band. The unequal high ends also appear reversed relative to SOURCE 1; camera handedness remains uncertain.
issues.action: Locally adjust the roof profile and corresponding upper glazing/support heights to restore the source-backed central clearance. Establish matching ramp-end orientation before assigning the higher roof edge; retain the existing lower building during this correction.

issues.problem: CURRENT 15 shows the upper diagonal ramp/rail assembly extending beyond the right enclosure edge without a clearly resolved landing connection. SOURCE 1–2 show ramp flights terminating at identifiable perimeter landings. Dense overlapping lines in CURRENT obscure whether these are connected joints or passing intersections.
issues.action: Review the ramp-end landing closeups against the source, then locally trim or connect only confirmed overshooting ramp and rail ends. Verify deck-to-landing contact and continuous guarding; do not treat projected overlap as a completed joint.

keep: The straight horizontal top edge of the outer glazed enclosure, separate from the curved roof.
The existing roof’s smooth concave curvature; retain that character while correcting its vertical profile.

assessment: Sources 1–2 establish the same elongated building through its curved roof, projecting glazed upper enclosure and zigzag ramps at the short end. Source 3 shows the recessed entrance and open grated gallery; source 4 shows the timber ceiling, circular floor openings, spiral stair and double-height lower workspace. Sources 5–8 corroborate the concrete frame, timber upper addition, perimeter buffer zone and unequal internal floor extents. CURRENT captures these broad systems, but the ramp direction, internal void configuration and gallery construction differ visibly. Exact dimensions are not supplied. Images 22–25 repeat uncut exterior views and cannot verify the source sections; screenshots also cannot establish concealed joints.

issues.problem: SOURCE 1–2 shows the lowest ramp descending toward the right, with alternating flights above. CURRENT 15–16 descends toward the left and reverses that defining end composition; the upper flight also projects beyond the enclosure without a clearly resolved landing connection.
issues.action: Locally correct the ramp flights’ direction and landing positions using the shared end-view landmarks. Connect each flight to its intended floor or gallery with continuous walking surfaces and guards; verify clearances at the glazed enclosure.

issues.problem: SOURCE 4–5 shows a substantial double-height workspace beside a partial intermediate floor. CURRENT 21 instead shows closely stacked horizontal beams and floor surfaces across that region, substantially reducing the observed vertical opening. CURRENT 20 also leaves a circular floor opening unguarded, unlike the source’s circular mesh guards.
issues.action: Correct only the intermediate floor extent and associated beams around the source-backed double-height void. Align the spiral stair with the actual floor openings and landings, and guard the exposed circular opening.

issues.problem: SOURCE 3 shows a light, open gallery with visible transverse steel beams and translucent/open grating overhead. CURRENT 19 replaces this with a broad opaque grey soffit and deep continuous edge, obscuring the source’s structural rhythm and openness.
issues.action: Locally revise the gallery deck, soffit and edge assembly to expose the observed beam-and-grating construction. Check inclined support endpoints against actual structural members rather than accepting apparent screen-space contact.

keep: The visible short-end roof edge’s concave profile, including its higher right endpoint in the matched end view.
The recessed ground-level column line beneath the projecting gallery.

assessment: SOURCE panels show one elongated building: a recessed lower frame, a projecting two-storey glazed buffer enclosure, perimeter decks, three alternating end-ramp flights, and a curved timber roof with unequal raised edges. Exterior photographs, the aerial drawing and physical-model views share these landmarks. Interior panels show the curved timber soffit, exposed frame and spiral circulation; plans and sections show floor openings and differing internal floor extents. CURRENT retains the recognizable exterior arrangement, but the roof trough sits too close to the enclosure’s top edge, and ramp terminations need correction or closer verification. No user-confirmed dimensions are supplied. These uncut exterior views cannot establish internal fidelity or prove physical connections; dark outlines alone do not establish incorrect materials.

issues.problem: SOURCE end views show a substantial glazed zone between the roof trough and the horizontal buffer-enclosure roofline. In CURRENT image 15, the trough nearly touches that roofline, compressing the defining upper-storey silhouette.
issues.action: Raise the central portion of the curved roof and adjust its adjoining glazing/support heights locally to restore the source-visible clearance. Preserve the right-higher edge relationship; do not protect the entire existing roof profile.

issues.problem: CURRENT image 15 shows the upper ramp/rail extending beyond the right enclosure edge and broad projecting pieces at the flight ends. SOURCE physical-model views show flights resolving into perimeter decks and defined landings. The current overlaps do not demonstrate continuous walking surfaces or correctly terminated rails.
issues.action: Locally align flight endpoints with their receiving decks, trim unsupported overruns, and resolve landing surfaces and rail returns. Verify the joints in close views before accepting them; preserve correctly positioned flight portions.

keep: Right roof edge higher than the left in the matched ramp-end orientation.
